Pregnancy

Gas and air in labour: nitrous oxide, pain relief and safety

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Gas and air can make contractions easier to cope with while you remain awake and control a mask or mouthpiece. It usually provides less pain relief than an epidural, and you can change your mind. Safe use means a medical nitrous oxide–oxygen mixture, an individual suitability check and trained maternity staff; it is not a home treatment using recreational gas.

What is in labour gas?

The active gas is nitrous oxide, N2O, sometimes called laughing gas. It is not nitrogen, nitric oxide or a nitrate. Entonox and many labour systems provide a fixed mixture of 50% nitrous oxide and 50% oxygen. Despite the name ‘gas and air’, this is a controlled medical mixture rather than ordinary room air.

The aim is to reduce pain and anxiety without making you unconscious. Relief starts and fades quickly because the gas enters and leaves through the lungs. It does not numb the lower body like an epidural, and it does not reliably remove every sensation or make everyone laugh.

How the self-held mask and timing work

A midwife or other trained professional explains the equipment and coaches your breathing. With the usual labour system, you hold the mask or mouthpiece yourself and breathe through a demand valve. A partner should not hold the mask onto your face, and it should not be strapped on. Being able to understand instructions and hold it independently is part of the suitability assessment.

The effect is not instantaneous: teams commonly coach starting at the beginning of, or just before, an expected contraction. NHS information describes about 15–20 seconds to work; ASA guidance describes starting about 30 seconds before a contraction. These are practical guides, not a stopwatch target. Follow the team's coaching, including how to breathe out through its system, rather than trying to predict contractions from a monitor yourself.

Where it is available and what care it needs

Availability varies between countries, hospitals, birth centres and supported home-birth services. NICE recommends Entonox availability in all birth settings within its UK care framework; that is not a promise that every local service provides it. Ask before labour, including what happens if you need transfer for an epidural or another form of care.

Staff need suitable medical equipment, training, observation and a plan for responding to problems. Ventilation and collection of exhaled gas help protect staff from repeated workplace exposure. Monitoring is chosen for your health, labour and any other medicines; the gas does not cancel routine maternal or baby checks. Do not obtain cylinders, adjust mixtures or set up a home supply yourself.

How much pain relief should you expect?

Many people describe partial relief or feeling better able to cope rather than pain disappearing. Epidural analgesia generally provides stronger pain relief. Research on nitrous oxide is less robust and results vary; satisfaction also reflects control, support, expectations and the overall birth experience. Satisfaction and a low pain score are different outcomes.

A 2017 report from one centre studied vaginal births during 2011–2014: 1,246 of 6,507 women receiving anaesthetic care initially chose nitrous oxide, about 19%. Of those 1,246, 753, or 60%, used nitrous oxide alone and 493 switched to neuraxial analgesia. These are selected observational figures, not a universal popularity rate or a 60% chance of painless birth. The study did not establish that gas gives everyone greater satisfaction than an epidural.

Control, movement and changing your mind

Some people value avoiding a needle-based technique initially, holding their own mask and stopping when they wish. Others dislike the mask or find the relief insufficient. Choosing another method is not a failure. The best choice can change as contractions, fatigue, labour progress or your preferences change.

Gas does not deliberately block leg strength, but dizziness, sleepiness, other medicines and the clinical situation can make standing unsafe. Check with your midwife before walking or changing position, and ask for help if unsteady. Claims that gas always permits unrestricted movement, never sedates or is the fastest and best method for everyone are misleading.

Switching treatments is different from combining them

Tell the team about all medicines, alcohol or other substances, including a recent opioid injection or a sedating medicine. ACOG's advisory, reaffirmed in 2025, and ASA guidance advise against combining labour nitrous oxide with systemic opioids or sedative/hypnotic medicines because sedation and breathing suppression may increase. Do not take an extra painkiller or sleeping medicine on your own while using it.

The team can plan a safe transition to another method, including an epidural, taking previous medicines and your condition into account. Gas may be considered while another plan is arranged, but this is not permission to add it to any treatment without review. If an epidural is not relieving pain, tell the anaesthesia team so it can be assessed. A caesarean or a substantial repair needs appropriate anaesthesia, not gas alone.

Side effects and when to stop

Nausea, vomiting, lightheadedness, dizziness, drowsiness, disorientation or an unpleasant enclosed feeling from the mask can occur. Tell the staff, remove the mask or mouthpiece and let them reassess you; many ordinary effects settle quickly after stopping. Do not keep inhaling to push through feeling unwell or stand up while dizzy.

Difficulty breathing, becoming difficult to wake, loss of consciousness or a seizure needs immediate help from the clinical team, rather than being treated as an expected effect. Stop inhaling and alert staff immediately; a companion should call for help if you cannot. Symptoms that persist after stopping also need assessment. Feeling clearer quickly is not automatic clearance to drive, care for a baby alone or leave care.

Conditions the team needs to know about

Nitrous oxide can expand gas trapped inside the body. Tell the anaesthetist about a collapsed lung, a bowel obstruction or marked abdominal distension, and recent eye surgery with an injected gas bubble; the bubble must be fully absorbed before exposure is considered. Recent ear procedures, facial injury, impaired consciousness and difficulty holding a mask also matter. Do not decide suitability from a short online checklist.

Significant heart or lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, a need for supplemental oxygen, intoxication and other medicines require individual specialist assessment. Pulmonary hypertension means high pressure in the lung circulation, not low pressure. A mental-health diagnosis by itself is not a universal ban; current ability to consent, cooperate, use the mask and remain safe is what the team must assess.

Why vitamin B12 and exposure duration matter

Nitrous oxide inactivates vitamin B12. Known B12 deficiency or pernicious anaemia should be disclosed before labour; a vegan or poorly supplemented diet, anaemia or bowel surgery may prompt assessment for deficiency. Testing is considered according to risk, not automatically required for everyone. Do not assume a normal blood count excludes a problem or that taking a vitamin immediately beforehand guarantees protection.

Prolonged or repeated exposure increases concern for blood and nerve effects, but rare neurological toxicity has also been reported after a single anaesthetic exposure in people with unrecognised deficiency. Staff must review unusually long or repeated use and arrange appropriate monitoring or alternatives. New persistent tingling, numbness, weakness or difficulty walking after exposure needs prompt medical assessment, with the gas exposure mentioned.

Effects on labour and the baby

Available studies have not shown a clear adverse effect on usual labour progress or immediate newborn measures such as Apgar scores and cord blood gases when nitrous oxide is used appropriately. That does not prove it prevents assisted birth or caesarean birth, or that every short- and long-term outcome is known. Evidence on long-term development and some vulnerable groups is limited. A large matched observational cohort published in 2026 also reported a higher neonatal intensive-care admission rate after nitrous oxide exposure. This association does not prove that the gas caused the admissions.

Nitrous oxide crosses the placenta; it is not simply filtered out by the placenta or eliminated by fetal urine. Its rapid removal after inhalation stops helps explain the reassuring immediate observations, but ‘no possible effect on the baby’ is too strong. Labour analgesia is also different from an anaesthetic procedure earlier in pregnancy. The product information does not establish a blanket first-trimester prohibition; any earlier procedure needs its own benefit–risk assessment.

After birth, repairs and breastfeeding

The team may offer inhaled analgesia for selected examinations or procedures after birth, sometimes alongside an appropriately planned local or regional technique. A painful perineal repair still needs tested, effective anaesthesia; do not feel obliged to tolerate pain because gas is available. Tell the professional if the procedure hurts.

LactMed states that nitrous oxide alone does not require a breastfeeding waiting period or discarding milk because it clears quickly. With general anaesthesia or several medicines, recovery and the other drugs determine advice; breastfeed when sufficiently recovered to do so safely, with help if needed. Evidence does not justify promising better breastfeeding or assuming a sleepy parent can safely hold a baby without assistance.

Questions for your birth plan

Ask whether gas is available at your planned setting, who will explain and observe its use, which health conditions or medicines may change the plan, and what alternatives are available if it is unpleasant or ineffective. Discuss transfer arrangements and your priorities: stronger pain relief, mobility, avoiding needles initially or keeping a sense of control.

Record relevant B12 history, previous gas or anaesthetic reactions, eye surgery, lung problems and medicines for the team. You can revise your preference during labour. A written plan supports conversation; it does not replace reassessment when your condition changes, and safety concerns should be raised immediately rather than saved for the next appointment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Discuss local availability, B12 history, medical conditions and medicines with your maternity team before labour.

Ask how to stop, whom to alert and which alternatives are available; reassess the plan whenever symptoms or preferences change.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to prepare your birth-plan questions and a concise medicine and health-history list. It cannot check equipment, decide whether gas is suitable for you or replace observation and advice from your maternity and anaesthesia teams.

When to seek help

Use only the clinical team's medical gas system and hold the mask yourself. Stop inhaling and alert staff immediately for difficulty breathing, difficulty waking, loss of consciousness or a seizure. Do not independently combine gas with opioids, sleeping medicines or other sedatives. Persistent neurological symptoms after exposure need prompt assessment. Do not drive or handle the baby alone while impaired.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Labour gas is a medical nitrous oxide–oxygen mixture used with trained staff.
  • It often helps coping but gives less pain relief than an epidural; switching is allowed.
  • Hold the mask yourself and follow coaching; do not use a home or recreational supply.
  • Disclose B12 risks, trapped-gas conditions and all medicines, especially opioids or sedatives.
  • Immediate newborn observations are reassuring, but universal or long-term safety guarantees are not justified.

Frequently asked questions

Who may not be able to use gas and air?

People with certain trapped-gas conditions, significant B12 deficiency, impaired consciousness or inability to use the mask independently may need another option. Recent eye-gas surgery, serious heart or lung disease and other medicines require assessment. This is an individual clinical decision, not a blanket ban for every mental-health diagnosis.

Will it make labour painless?

Usually not. It may reduce pain or help you cope while you remain aware of contractions. An epidural generally provides stronger analgesia. You may stop or ask for a different option; the historical 60% figure describes one cohort's use without switching, not painless births.

How should I time the breaths?

Your midwife coaches you with the actual system, usually beginning at the start of or just before an expected contraction because the effect takes several seconds. Hold the mask or mouthpiece yourself. A partner should not hold it onto your face, and you should not alter equipment settings.

Can I combine it with an opioid injection or sleeping medicine?

Do not combine these yourself. Current ACOG and ASA advice discourages coadministration with systemic opioids or sedative/hypnotic medicines because of deeper sedation and breathing suppression. Tell the team what you have already taken so it can plan a safe alternative or transition.

What if I feel sick, dizzy or very sleepy?

Stop inhaling, tell the staff and avoid standing unassisted. Many ordinary effects fade quickly. Difficulty breathing, difficulty waking, loss of consciousness or a seizure requires immediate clinical help; do not wait for all signs or dismiss them as normal gas effects.

Does it affect the baby or the course of birth?

Studies of appropriately used labour gas have generally been reassuring for immediate newborn measures and have not shown a clear effect on usual labour progress. The gas crosses the placenta, and long-term evidence is limited. It does not guarantee avoidance of an assisted or caesarean birth. A large matched observational cohort published in 2026 also reported a higher neonatal intensive-care admission rate after nitrous oxide exposure. This association does not prove that the gas caused the admissions.

Do I need to discard breast milk afterwards?

Not for nitrous oxide alone, according to LactMed. If other medicines or general anaesthesia were used, follow the advice for those medicines and your recovery. Get help holding or feeding the baby if you remain drowsy or unsteady.

Can I arrange my own supply for a home birth?

No. If a supported home-birth service offers gas, its trained team must provide and manage the appropriate medical system and safety arrangements. Availability and transfer plans vary. Recreational products, cylinders obtained independently and improvised mixing are not substitutes.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
